text:
“Ève! Ève!” David replied, “I wish I could be Lucien’s brother.
You alone can give me that title, which would allow him to accept everything from me, which would give me the right to devote myself to him with the holy love you bring to your sacrifices, but with the discernment of a calculating man as well. Ève, dear beloved child, give Lucien a treasure from which he can draw without shame. Will not a brother’s purse be as his own? If you knew all the thoughts Lucien’s new position has prompted in me! If he wishes to visit Madame de Bargeton, he must no longer be my foreman, he must no longer live in L’Houmeau, you must no longer remain a working girl, your mother must no longer ply her trade. If you consented to become my wife, everything would be smoothed out: Lucien could live on the second floor of my house while I built him an apartment above the lean-to at the back of the courtyard, unless my father is willing to add another story. In this way we would arrange for him a life free of care, an independent life. My desire to support Lucien will give me a courage to make my fortune that I would not have if only I myself were concerned; but it is for you to authorize my devotion. Perhaps one day he will go to Paris, the only stage on which he can make himself known, and where his talents will be appreciated and rewarded. Life in Paris is expensive, and the three of us will not be too many to support him there. Besides, will not you and your mother need someone to rely on? Dear Ève, marry me for love of Lucien. Later, perhaps you will love me when you see the efforts I shall make to serve him and to make you happy. We are both equally modest in our tastes; we shall need very little. Lucien’s happiness will be our great concern, and his heart will be the treasure in which we shall place fortune, feelings, sensations—everything!”

“Propriety separates us,” said Ève, moved to see how humble this great love made itself. “You are rich and I am poor. One must love deeply to overcome such a difficulty.”

“Then you do not yet love me enough?” cried David, aghast.

“But your father might oppose it...”

“Good, good,” David replied. “If my father is the only one to be consulted, you shall be my wife. Ève, my dear Ève! You have just made life very easy for me to bear at this moment. Alas, my heart was very heavy with feelings that I could neither express nor knew how to express. Only tell me that you love me a little, and I shall summon the courage needed to speak to you of all the rest.”

“Truly,” she said, “you make me feel quite ashamed; but since we are confiding our feelings to each other, I shall tell you that never in my life have I thought of anyone but you. I saw in you one of those men to whom a woman may be proud to belong, and I did not dare hope for myself, a poor working girl with no future, so great a destiny.”

“Enough, enough,” he said, sitting down on the crossbeam of the dam beside which they had returned, for they had been pacing back and forth like mad people over the same stretch of ground.

“What is the matter?” she asked him, expressing for the first time that graceful concern women feel for a being who belongs to them.

“Nothing but good,” he said. “When one catches sight of an entire happy life, the mind is as though dazzled, the soul overwhelmed. Why am I the happier of us?” he said with a melancholy expression. “But I know why.”

Ève looked at David with a coquettish, questioning air that demanded an explanation.

“Dear Ève, I receive more than I give. And so I shall always love you more than you will love me, because I have more reason to love you: you are an angel and I am a man.”

“I am not so learned,” Ève replied with a smile. “I love you dearly...”

“As much as you love Lucien?” he said, interrupting her.

“Enough to be your wife, to devote myself to you, and to try to cause you no sorrow in the life—somewhat difficult at first—that we shall lead.”

“Have you noticed, dear Ève, that I have loved you since the first day I saw you?”

“What woman does not feel when she is loved?” she asked.

“Then let me dispel the scruples caused in you by my supposed wealth. I am poor, my dear Ève. Yes, my father took pleasure in ruining me; he speculated on my labor; he behaved as many supposed benefactors do toward those indebted to them. If I become rich, it will be through you. This is not a lover’s declaration, but a thinker’s reflection. I must make my faults known to you, and they are enormous in a man obliged to make his fortune. My character, my habits, and the occupations that please me make me unfit for everything involving trade and speculation, and yet we can become rich only by engaging in some industry. Though I am capable of discovering a gold mine, I am singularly inept at exploiting it. But you, who, out of love for your brother, have descended to the smallest details, who possess a genius for economy and the patient attentiveness of the true merchant—you will reap the harvest I have sown. Our situation—for a long time now I have counted myself as part of your family—weighs so heavily upon my heart that I have spent my days and nights seeking an opportunity to make our fortune. My knowledge of chemistry and my observation of the needs of commerce have put me on the path to a lucrative discovery. I cannot yet tell you anything about it; I foresee too many delays. We may suffer for several years, but in the end I shall discover the industrial processes whose trail I have been following for the past few days and which will bring us a great fortune. I have said nothing to Lucien, for his ardent nature would spoil everything; he would turn my hopes into realities, live like a great lord, and perhaps run into debt. So keep my secret for me. Your sweet and dear companionship alone will be able to console me during these long trials, just as the desire to enrich you and Lucien will give me steadfastness and tenacity...”

“I had also guessed,” Ève said, interrupting him, “that you were one of those inventors who, like my poor father, need a woman to take care of them.”

“Then you love me! Ah, tell me so without fear—to me, who have seen in your name a symbol of my love. Eve was the only woman in the world, and what was materially true for Adam is morally true for me. My God! Do you love me?”

“Yes,” she said, drawing out that simple syllable in the way she pronounced it, as though to portray the breadth of her feelings.

“Well then, let us sit here,” he said, leading Ève by the hand toward a long beam at the foot of the wheels of a paper mill. “Let me breathe the evening air, hear the cries of the tree frogs, admire the moonbeams trembling on the water; let me take possession of this nature in which I seem to see my happiness written in everything, and which appears to me for the first time in its splendor, illuminated by love, made beautiful by you. Ève, dear beloved! This is the first moment of unalloyed joy fate has ever given me! I doubt that Lucien is as happy as I am!”
